title: Archaeology of the City: Urban Planning in Ancient Israel and Its Social Implications
author: Ze'ev Herzog
publisher: Tel Aviv University, Institute of Archaeology
allowedUseNotes: Copyrighted monograph. Summaries in project's own words only.
summary: Urban-form study covering, among much else, the early Iron Age 'enclosed settlement' plan (dwellings ringing an open center, e.g. Beersheba VII) used as the comparative model for the Ziklag placeholder layout. Also includes a regional gate-typology synthesis (pp. 231-291, gate discussion concentrated at pp. 287-291 per secondary citation) tracking Iron Age city-gate chamber counts across excavated Israelite/Levantine sites over time: two-chamber gates are the prevalent form in the 11th and early 10th centuries BCE (with a few four-chamber examples appearing at the very end of that span), before larger four- and six-chamber gates become common from the mid-10th century BCE onward (the type most associated, rightly or on a disputed 'Solomonic' dating, with monumental sites like Hazor, Megiddo, and Gezer).
